title: Ratio and Regression Estimators
breadcrumb: Sampling theory → Auxiliary information → Ratio and regression estimation
engineName: Use known population auxiliary information to adjust the sample mean of a study variable.
objectives: State and calculate ratio and regression estimators of a population mean.
Explain when proportional versus linear auxiliary relationships support each estimator.
Compute adjusted estimates using known population auxiliary means.
Interpret residual-based approximate variances under SRSWOR.
Explain why the ratio estimator is generally not exactly design-unbiased.

prereq.name: Population and sample means
prereq.why: Both estimators adjust the sample mean using a population benchmark.

prereq.name: Covariance and regression slope
prereq.why: The regression estimator uses the fitted sample slope.

prereq.name: Simple random sampling without replacement
prereq.why: The variance approximations use an SRSWOR design and its FPC.

traps: Ratio estimation scales ȳ by X̄/x̄; regression adds b(X̄−x̄).
Do not reverse the sign in the regression adjustment.
A ratio estimator is generally not exactly design-unbiased in finite samples.
The ratio estimator is most plausible for a proportional near-origin relationship.
State the sampling design before quoting a variance approximation.
howto: Identify the known population auxiliary mean X̄. Compare the relationship of y to x: use ratio estimation for an approximately proportional relationship and regression estimation for a linear relationship that may have an intercept. Write the formula before substitution. For variance, define residuals and state SRSWOR and first-order approximation assumptions.

scenes.title: Auxiliary information and sample means
scenes.objective: Refresh population means, sample means and known auxiliary totals.
body: A survey often measures an outcome y together with an auxiliary variable x. The auxiliary variable may be cheaper to collect, available from a register, or strongly related to y.
Write X̄ and Ȳ for the population means, and x̄ and ȳ for the corresponding sample means. Ratio and regression estimators use the known population information about x to improve estimation of y.
The sample is still selected under a probability design. Auxiliary information changes the estimator, not the sampling design itself.

items.recall: A variable related to the study variable and used to improve estimation.
refresh: An auxiliary variable x is measured on the same population units as y and is useful because it is related to the study variable. It may come from a register, an earlier census or a cheaper measurement operation. Its purpose is to improve precision, not to replace the variable y that defines the target.

items.recall: The known population mean of the auxiliary variable.
refresh: The population mean X̄ is the fixed mean of x over all N population units. In this lesson it is assumed known from an external source. It is not the sample mean and it does not change when a different sample is drawn; the sample mean x̄ is calculated only from the selected units.

items.ask: What is the sample mean of y?
refresh: The sample mean ȳ is the arithmetic average of the observed study values: add the y-values for the n sampled units and divide by n. Under SRSWOR it is design-unbiased for the finite-population mean Ȳ. Ratio and regression estimators adjust this starting value using the difference between known X̄ and observed x̄.

ask.q: Why can a known population mean of x help estimate the population mean of y?
ask.nudge: If x and y are related, the sample's x̄ signals whether the sample is high or low relative to the population benchmark.

scenes.title: Correct the sample using a benchmark
scenes.objective: Explain the ratio adjustment and its assumptions.
body: Suppose the sample average household size is 3, but the known population average is 4. If expenditure tends to increase in proportion to household size, the sample expenditure mean may be scaled upward by 4/3.
The ratio estimator multiplies ȳ by X̄/x̄. It is intuitive when the relationship between y and x is approximately proportional and passes near the origin.
A regression estimator instead adjusts by a slope and the difference X̄−x̄. It is more flexible when the relationship has a nonzero intercept.

scenario.title: Using a population benchmark
body: A survey team measures monthly expenditure and household size for a probability sample. The sample has an average household size of 3 persons and average monthly expenditure of ₹12,000. The latest population register gives a reliable average household size of 4 persons. If expenditure is roughly proportional to household size over the relevant range, the sample mean can be adjusted upward by the ratio 4/3. This adjustment does not invent extra observations; it uses a known population benchmark to correct the sample's auxiliary-variable imbalance. If the relationship is not proportional, a regression adjustment may be more appropriate.
The analyst must still consider the sampling design and the approximate nature of the ratio estimator's bias and variance formula.
scenario.q: What ratio estimate follows from these sample and population means?

ask.q: When is a ratio estimator especially plausible?
ask.nudge: When y and x are positively related and the relationship is approximately proportional through the origin.

scenes.title: See the ratio adjustment
scenes.objective: Compute a ratio estimate from a simple sample.

viz.caption: The adjustment factor X̄/x̄ is 4/3 when X̄=4 and x̄=3.

body: If X̄=x̄, the ratio estimator equals the ordinary sample mean ȳ; no auxiliary adjustment is needed.
If X̄ is larger than x̄, the ratio estimator scales ȳ upward. If X̄ is smaller, it scales ȳ downward.
For ȳ=12,000, x̄=3 and X̄=4, the adjustment factor is 1.333…, giving 16,000.

ask.q: If X̄/x̄=0.8 and ȳ=50, what is the ratio estimate?

scenes.title: Ratio and regression estimators
scenes.objective: State estimators and distinguish their adjustment mechanisms.

blocks.body: For a sample of size n, ȳ and x̄ are sample means. The known population auxiliary mean is X̄. The sample regression slope is b= s_xy/s_x².
Ȳ_R=ȳ(X̄/x̄). Equivalently, estimate the ratio R by r=ȳ/x̄ and use Ȳ_R=rX̄.
Ȳ_reg=ȳ+b(X̄−x̄). The sample mean is adjusted by the fitted slope times the auxiliary-mean discrepancy.
V(ȳ_R)≈(1−f)S_e²/n, where eᵢ=yᵢ−Rxᵢ. V(ȳ_reg)≈(1−f)S_{y·x}²/n, where residuals are yᵢ−α−βxᵢ. These are first-order approximations; the exact design variance depends on the design and estimator.

The ratio estimator is generally not exactly design-unbiased in finite samples. Its bias is often small for a strong near-origin relationship. The regression estimator also uses estimated coefficients and is generally treated through approximation. Choose using the relationship, auxiliary quality and design.

flow.title: Choose the auxiliary adjustment
flow.alt: Start with the sample mean, compare the sample auxiliary mean with its known population mean, then choose ratio scaling for a proportional relationship or regression adjustment for a linear relationship with an intercept.
flow.note: A strong auxiliary relationship can improve precision; it does not remove the need to state assumptions.

ask.q: What distinguishes the ratio adjustment from the regression adjustment?
ask.nudge: Ratio scales ȳ by X̄/x̄; regression adds b(X̄−x̄).

scenes.title: Worked ratio and regression estimates
scenes.objective: Calculate and compare both adjusted estimates.
scenes.problem: A sample has x̄=10 and ȳ=12. The known population auxiliary mean is X̄=15. Calculate the ratio estimate and the regression estimate when b=1.2.

steps.why: The sample auxiliary mean is two-thirds of the known population mean.

steps.say: Multiply the sample study mean by this factor.
steps.why: The ratio estimator scales the observed y mean by the auxiliary benchmark.

steps.say: For regression, calculate the auxiliary mean difference.
steps.why: This is the amount by which the sample auxiliary mean differs from the population benchmark.

steps.say: Multiply the difference by the slope and add it to ȳ.
steps.why: The regression estimator adjusts additively using the fitted slope.
They coincide for these chosen values, but the estimators are not generally identical.

ask.q: If the regression slope were 0.8 instead, what would the regression estimate be?

scenes.title: Retrieve the two formulas
scenes.objective: Recall the estimator forms and key assumptions.

items.q: What is the ratio estimator's main relationship assumption?
items.a: A strong approximately proportional relationship through the origin.

items.q: What does the regression adjustment multiply?
items.a: The difference X̄−x̄ by the fitted slope b.

scenes.title: Complete the estimator comparison
scenes.objective: Build both estimates from their components.
scenes.problem: Given ȳ=20, x̄=5, X̄=6 and b=2, complete the ratio and regression estimates.

steps.say: The ratio adjustment factor is X̄/x̄.
steps.why: The population auxiliary mean is 20% above the sample auxiliary mean.

steps.say: Multiply the sample y mean by the ratio factor.
steps.why: The ratio estimator scales the sample mean.
The regression adjustment uses this difference.

steps.say: Add b times the discrepancy to ȳ.
steps.why: The regression estimate is an additive adjustment.

ask.q: Why can the ratio and regression estimates differ?
ask.nudge: They use different functional relationships and different adjustments.

scenes.title: Approximate variance and bias
scenes.objective: Interpret residual-based variance and ratio bias.

blocks.body: For R=Ȳ/X̄, define eᵢ=yᵢ−Rxᵢ. Under SRSWOR, a first-order approximation is V(Ȳ_R)≈(1−f)S_e²/n.
For population regression coefficients α and β, define eᵢ=yᵢ−α−βxᵢ. The regression estimator's approximate variance is driven by residual variation after explaining y with x.
The ratio estimator is a nonlinear function of sample means, so it is generally biased in finite samples. Its first-order bias is approximately (1−f)/(nX̄) [R S_x²−S_xy], under SRSWOR conventions.

First identify whether X̄ or X is known. Then write the correct estimator, substitute the sample and population quantities, and state the design/approximation assumptions before using a variance formula.

ask.q: Why is the ratio estimator not generally exactly unbiased?
ask.nudge: It is a ratio of random sample quantities, and expectation of a ratio is not generally the ratio of expectations.

scenes.title: Guided practice: select the estimator
scenes.objective: Choose and calculate an estimator from the relationship.
scenes.problem: A sample has ȳ=30, x̄=6, and the known population mean X̄=8. The relationship is approximately proportional. Find the ratio estimate and explain the choice.
scenes.answer: Ȳ_R=30×(8/6)=40. Ratio estimation is suitable because the relationship is approximately proportional.

scenario.title: Register acreage as auxiliary information
body: A crop survey estimates average yield per holding. A sample of farms provides observed yields and acreage, while an agricultural register supplies the population mean acreage. The sample mean acreage is lower than the known population mean, and yield is approximately proportional to acreage for the crop and region under study. A ratio adjustment can therefore correct the sample mean yield using the acreage benchmark. The analyst must not assume the same adjustment is appropriate if yield has a substantial fixed component unrelated to acreage; in that case a regression estimator with an intercept may be more suitable.
The choice should be justified by the empirical relationship and the quality of the population auxiliary information, rather than by the availability of a convenient formula alone.
scenario.q: Which estimator is suggested by an approximately proportional relationship?

solution.say: The proportional relationship supports ratio estimation.

ask.q: What should be checked before using the ratio estimator?
ask.nudge: That x̄ is nonzero and the y–x relationship is plausibly proportional.

scenes.title: Avoid common estimator traps
scenes.objective: Distinguish estimator forms and inference claims.

items.why: It scales the sample mean by the known-to-sample auxiliary mean ratio.
The sign is reversed; the adjustment is b(X̄−x̄).

items.claim: The ratio estimator is exactly design-unbiased for every finite population.
items.why: It is generally biased because it is a nonlinear ratio of random sample quantities.

items.claim: If X̄=x̄, both displayed adjusted estimators reduce to ȳ.
items.why: The ratio factor is one and the regression adjustment is zero.

items.claim: Ratio estimation is most natural for a proportional relationship through the origin.
items.why: A near-origin proportional relationship supports scaling by X̄/x̄.

items.claim: Regression adjustment requires the slope b to be multiplied by X̄−x̄.
items.why: This is the additive correction in the regression estimator.

scenes.title: Transfer: regression with an intercept
scenes.objective: Apply regression adjustment when proportionality is unsuitable.
scenes.problem: A sample gives ȳ=50 and x̄=10; the known population mean is X̄=12. A fitted regression slope is b=1.5. Calculate the regression estimate and explain why it can be preferred to a ratio estimate.
hints: Add the result to ȳ; explain the role of an intercept.
scenes.answer: Ȳ_reg=50+1.5(12−10)=53. Regression can be preferred when the relationship is approximately linear but does not pass through the origin.
scenes.check: The auxiliary difference is 2 and the adjustment is 3.

solution.say: The population auxiliary mean exceeds the sample mean by 2.
The fitted slope converts that difference into an estimated y adjustment of 3.
Add the adjustment to 50 to obtain 53.
A regression line can accommodate a nonzero intercept, unlike a strict proportional model.

ask.q: What feature of the relationship makes regression more flexible?

scenes.title: Formula and decision checklist
body: Ratio estimator: Ȳ_R=ȳ(X̄/x̄). Use when y is approximately proportional to x and x̄ is nonzero.
Regression estimator: Ȳ_reg=ȳ+b(X̄−x̄). Use when a linear relationship with a possible nonzero intercept is plausible.
Under SRSWOR, first-order approximate variances are residual-based and include the FPC (1−f). State the design and approximation before using them.
The ratio estimator is generally not exactly design-unbiased in finite samples. Auxiliary information can improve precision when it is reliable and strongly related to y.
Exam sequence: identify known population auxiliary information, choose the relationship form, write the estimator, substitute carefully, and state bias/variance qualifications.

ask.q: Which estimator and key design condition should you remember for Ratio and Regression Estimators?
ask.nudge: State the estimator, its weighting or expansion rule, and the assumptions behind its variance.

scenes.title: Mastery check
scenes.objective: Demonstrate independent command of ratio and regression estimators.

sheet: Ratio estimator generally has finite-sample bias.
cards: X̄ is the known population mean of x; x̄ is calculated from the sample.
tricks: Check whether x̄ is nonzero before ratio estimation.
For regression, calculate X̄−x̄ before multiplying by b.
Use the known population mean, not the sample mean, in the adjustment.
shortcuts: If X̄=x̄, both adjustments reduce to ȳ.
A proportional relationship points to ratio; a nonzero intercept points to regression.
Calculate r=ȳ/x̄ once; the ratio estimate is rX̄.
remember: Auxiliary information improves precision only when informative and reliable.
Approximate variance formulas need stated design assumptions.
